entries.note: A 'Silicon Valley Financial Crisis brewing' has no shared threshold or specified outcome.

entries.test: Ramp's customer spending data and historical concentration figures would establish whether the top 1% generated 80% of enterprise revenue without improvement over three years.
entries.note: He asserts the finding in his own voice while crediting Ramp.
The customer count is explicitly qualified as 'likely'; the revenue shares are separately checkable factual components.

entries.test: Subscription allowances, model pricing and reported token costs for the startups covered in his research would show whether virtually all allow consumption far above subscription prices while paying near-full token rates.
entries.note: The scope is the cases he has found, not every AI startup.

entries.test: Public revenue and usage data around model launches, alongside subscription subsidies and venture funding, would test whether subsidized use drives recurring launch-related revenue surges.
entries.note: This asserts a causal mechanism rather than merely a possible outcome.

entries.test: Customer concentration disclosures and startup financial reports would show whether the labs materially depend on customers whose token purchases require continued external funding.
entries.note: In context, 'isn't real revenue' means funding-dependent revenue, not nonexistent receipts.

entries.test: If the cited startups lose external funding, their financial results and continued model offerings would show whether they can sustain those offerings and whether token costs dominate their losses.
entries.note: Loss of funding is a prospective condition that could occur publicly.
Both the spending estimate and its potential disappearance are explicitly probabilistic.

entries.test: Customer financial statements, token spending and financing records would test whether rising payments require increasing external funding across every AI startup.
entries.note: The universal 'every single' is a substantive, testable commitment.
The original says NVIDIA wants Perplexity to keep spending; the normalization instead makes NVIDIA the spender. 'No logical or rational basis' is an evaluative judgment.

entries.test: Representative enterprise AI purchasing data classified by industry and startup profitability would show whether tech companies constitute the vast majority of buyers outside unprofitable AI startups.
entries.note: The assertion concerns the composition of buyers, not merely their share of spending.
'Prime targets' supplies neither a migration prediction nor an agreed measure of susceptibility. The sentence presents that susceptibility as a cause of exposure.

entries.test: Annual AI compute contracts and spending disclosures excluding OpenAI and Anthropic would establish the approximate total and the shares attributable to Jane Street and NVIDIA.
entries.note: An approximate numerical estimate remains checkable; he presents $22 billion as his closest estimate.

entries.test: Following any release of the labs' committed capacity, replacement contracts would show whether other buyers absorb that compute at comparable scale.
entries.note: The context concerns replacement demand at the labs' scale, not whether any individual GPU finds another buyer.

entries.test: Disclosed compute agreements and their contract values would show whether OpenAI and Anthropic's combined commitments exceed $1.3 trillion.
entries.note: The amount refers to contracted future revenue, not revenue already recognized.

entries.test: Published 2027 revenue estimates, lab financing requirements and customer spending disclosures would test both the $200 billion expectation and its asserted dependence on funding and concentrated customer growth.
entries.note: It describes current expectations and their financial dependencies, rather than claiming the revenue has already been earned.

entries.test: Compute payment schedules and annual expenses would show whether obligations ramp up substantially in 2027 and increase dramatically in subsequent years.
entries.note: The parenthetical doubts the industry's survival; the scheduled payment ramp is asserted firmly.

entries.test: A representative sample of contemporary AI reporting would show whether coverage overwhelmingly emphasizes favorable financial numbers while omitting adverse ones.
entries.note: The broad wording still makes a testable assertion about reporting patterns.
The operative inference explicitly uses 'will likely mean'.

entries.test: The reported projection and annual compute spending through 2030 would test the stated $750 billion total and inferred annual spending of at least $250 billion.
entries.note: He adopts the annual spending inference in his own voice; 'suggests' introduces a numerical inference rather than an explicit chance.

entries.test: The labs' cash balances, financing, operating cash flows and contractual payment schedules would show whether they lack funds for obligations and have kept current only because initial payments are small.
entries.note: Private-company financial information could become public; its current availability does not determine checkability.

entries.test: GPU buyers' cash flows, data center expenditures and debt issuance would show whether sustained purchases require substantial borrowing for every buyer except Microsoft.
entries.note: 'Near-infinite' is hyperbole, but the asserted necessity of debt has a clear factual reading.

entries.test: GPU capacity allocations, customer contracts and attributable revenues would show whether OpenAI and Anthropic drive almost all financial returns and most capacity expansion across the named buyers.
entries.note: 'Driven almost entirely by' asserts a causal dependence.

entries.test: Bloomberg's reporting and Microsoft's FY2026 AI revenue breakdown would establish whether approximately $10 billion of $33.33 billion came from customers other than OpenAI.
entries.note: The surrounding discussion identifies OpenAI as the excluded customer. The demand inference is anchored to this numerical comparison.

entries.test: Following an AI investment bust, bankruptcy filings and financial disclosures would show whether it caused either company to go bankrupt, while Broadcom's revenue disclosures would test the stated customer dependence.
entries.note: FY2028 dates the revenue estimate, not the bankruptcy prediction.
This summarizes an asserted chain of financial dependence rather than empty rhetoric. The customer count is explicitly hedged with 'maybe'.
